newsitem.title: THAILAND: Rising oil prices could hurt Thailand - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Rising oil prices could hurt Thailand - analysts.

text.p: Rising crude oil prices could put more pressure on Thailand's already slowing economy, particularly given its status as a net oil importer, analysts said on Thursday.
The price for Oman crude, the main type of Thai crude imports, has averaged US$17.78 per barrel so far this year compared with $15.09 in 1995, market sources said.
An increase of $1.00 or $2.00 in oil prices would normally be considered a potential problem to any economy, more so that of a net importer like Thailand, analysts told Reuters.
Thailand buys crude oil mainly from the Middle East and some from the Far East. The specifications of Middle East crude oil serve as a basic design for Thai refineries.
Despite the political and economic volatility of the Middle East, Thai policy makers say they still view oil prices from the region to be relatively stable.
Thailand's oil import bill in 1995 was 115.2 billion baht (US$4.6 billion), compared with non-oil imports of 1.67 trillion baht.
Paul Alapat, an economist with Lehman Brothers, said rising oil prices could worsen Thailand's fragile trade and current account deficits, already among the highest in the region.

Thailand's 1996 current account deficit is officially expected to total 7.8 percent of gross domestic product (GDP). Lehman, however, expects the deficit to be 8.5 percent of GDP, after 8.1 percent in 1995.
"It (the rise in oil prices) is bad for sentiment. But we do not plan to revise our current account deficit forecast for Thailand yet," Alapat said.
Thailand's economy has slowed sharply this year, with some private analysts expecting GDP growth to slow to just over 6.0 percent from the 8.6 percent posted in 1995.

Arporn Chewakrengkai, chief economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said higher oil prices were already factored into the group's economic forecasts, but warned Deutsche was likely to revise up the inflation forecast if oil prices rose steeply.
Recent Iraq-U.S. tensions have given rise to fears about which way oil prices might trend in the near future.
"Our forecast for 1996 inflation is 5.7 percent. But if oil prices remain at this high level, we might revise the forecast up to 6.0 percent," she said.
But Bhasu Phanich Supapol, president of SCB Research Institute, said there were sufficient stocks held in Thailand to weather the effects of any immediate rise in oil prices.
"The effect could be delayed or reduced. The stocks could at least give some room for the industry to delay importing crude if the prices continue to rise," he said.
